newsitem.title: USA: Brazil's short-term debt worries U.S. economists.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's short-term debt worries U.S. economists.

text.p: Brazil braved Tuesday's slump in stock and bond prices, but U.S. economists saw trouble ahead, not so much from its overvalued real currency or trade deficit, but from its massive stockpile of short-term domestic debt.

Brazil, despite sitting on close to $60 billion international reserves, could suffer greatly should investors lose confidence in the government's economic program, said University of Maryland Economics Professor Guillermo Calvo.

"There is a potential for problems, not because fundamentals are bad, but because they have not been careful enough about the maturity of the debt," said Calvo, who was credited with having forecast Mexico's 1994 peso devaluation.
Calvo noted that Brazilian policymakers were addressing the problem, but the average maturity of domestic debt, at only six months, was still too short.

An official report issued Wednesday said that as of April 1997, short-term domestic debt of the federal government and central bank, but not the state governments, totaled about 100 billion reais, or about $93 billion.
"Is there a crisis in the offing? My answer is that it depends on Wall Street's mood," Calvo said. "If they get nervous, then there could be a run."

Nerves may have been frayed on Tuesday, when fears that Brazil might be forced to devalue sparked a profit-taking binge that sent the Bovespa stock index .BVSP down 8.51 percent and Brazilian Brady bonds sharply lower.
Brazilian policymakers vowed to maintain its exchange rate policy, and the markets cut their losses on Wednesday.

Economists drew distinctions between Brazil and 1995 conditions in Mexico when the government, faced with depleted reserves, found its devaluation prompted investors to bail out of short-term dollar-denominated debt totaling $29 billion.
Principally, Brazil's short-term notes were denominated in reais and owned mostly by local investors.

"Brazilians may be less likely to dump the paper, not so much because Brazilians are slower or more generous, but simply because they have other uses for it," said Andres Velasco, professor of economics at New York University. "It serves liquidity needs."
Velasco said Brazil's situation was vulnerable, but the country could still pull off a soft landing that would involve approval of key measures to cut fiscal spending.

"If the market perceives fundamentals are okay, then the central bank can afford to lower interest rates, and let the currency depreciate a little bit," Velasco said, noting this to be the most likely, but not the only, scenario.

Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso reaffirmed Wednesday his commitment to balance the public accounts, and the government said all privatization proceeds would be dedicated to retire public sector debt.

But Nariman Behravesh, chief international economist at DRI/McGraw Hill, said Brazil's major problem was its failure to trim the budget deficit, leading the government to check inflation through higher interest rates.

"This combination of loose fiscal policy and tight monetary policy is unsustainable," Behravesh said. "How it resolves itself, in a Mexican style crisis or another style crisis, is a little hard to tell."

Behravesh said Brasilia faced several options: tighten interest rates, which might throw the economy into recession; devalue the currency; or slap on capital controls and raise tarriff walls. He said the government would most likely employ rates coupled with some form of capital controls.

But Calvo and Velasco noted other factors would help Brazil avoid a Mexico-style crisis. Brazil has already undergone a banking sector consolidation, and its political scene is far more stable than Mexico's was three years ago.
